label: Chapter 1: A Settlement in the Marsh

units.text: Every city has an origin story, and the story of Brussels begins with mud.
The river is called the Senne.
It is a small, slow stream that once wandered across a wide, wet valley in the middle of what is now Belgium, splitting into channels and forming islands as it went.
People have lived along the edges of that valley for a very long time.
Archaeologists have found traces of Iron Age settlers in the Brussels area, at a site called Champ Saint-Anne in the neighborhood of Anderlecht.
Roman farms and country houses were scattered across the surrounding countryside, though the Romans never built a real town on the spot.
After the Roman Empire faded, Frankish settlers moved in.
In the same field in Anderlecht, a Frankish cemetery with more than three hundred graves has been uncovered, dating from roughly the years 500 to 700.
These were farmers and fighters, living in small villages on the dry ground above the river, in the new Frankish kingdom that would eventually grow into the empire of Charlemagne.
Now comes the part where history shades into legend.
Tradition says that around the year 580, a holy man named Gaugericus, known in French as Saint Géry, who was bishop of the city of Cambrai, built a small chapel on an island in the Senne.
Historians are cautious about this story, because the sources are later and less certain.
But it is a good candidate for the seed of the city.
The place is still there. It is a square in the old center called Place Saint-Géry, and a former market hall stands on it, close to where the island once was.
The name Brussels itself points to the landscape.
In its earliest forms, it appears as something like Bruocsella, and most scholars read it as meaning a home in the marsh, or a dwelling by the swamp.
It is not a grand name. It is the name a farmer would give to a wet piece of ground.
And it tells us something true about this place: it began as a settlement that had to deal with water.
So why did a town grow here at all?
The answer is geography. The Senne valley sat on an important route.
Trade roads ran from the rich cloth-making cities of Flanders in the west to Cologne and the Rhine in the east.

Merchants carrying wool, cloth, wine, and metalwork passed through this region, and a spot where a river could be crossed or where boats could be brought upstream was a natural place to stop, unload, and do business.
The islands in the Senne offered safe ground.
The hills to the east offered a good place for a fortress.
For several centuries, the settlement was just a small place within a much larger political world.

In the ninth century, Charlemagne's empire was divided among his heirs, and the region that would become Belgium found itself caught in the middle, in a long, contested territory known as Lotharingia, named for the Frankish king Lothar.
The area went back and forth between the western and eastern halves of the old empire.
Later, the dukes who ruled Lotharingia on behalf of the German emperors kept a loose grip, and local lords held most of the real power.
Then, in the late tenth century, we get our first clear date.
In 977, the German emperor Otto the Second gave the duchy of Lower Lotharingia, which is roughly today's Belgium and part of the Netherlands, to a man named Charles.
Charles was a member of the old Carolingian family, a son of a French king, and a brother of the reigning French king.
He was an exile from the throne of France, looking for a power base.
Within a couple of years, he built a fortification on one of the islands in the Senne, the same island with the old chapel.
In about the year 979, Charles did something else that mattered even more.
He moved the relics of a saint named Gudula, a pious woman from the seventh century, to the chapel on the island.
Gudula became the patron saint of Brussels, and that move is the date most often given as the official founding of the city.
The tradition goes that Gudula was a noblewoman who loved to go to church before dawn, carrying a lantern, and that the devil kept blowing out her light, and each time an angel lit it again.
A caution is in order. Modern historians point out that the story of Charles building a castle and founding the city is based on sources written long after the fact.
The real picture is likely messier, with a growing settlement, a chapel, a market, and local lords all developing over several generations.
But 979 is the date that stuck, and Brussels celebrated its thousandth birthday in 1979.
Gudula's story had another long-term effect.

In 1047, a powerful nobleman, Lambert the Second, Count of Leuven, which is a city about twenty-five kilometers to the east, moved her relics again, this time to a new church on a hill overlooking the river valley.
He founded a college of priests there, called canons, to serve the church.
That hill church, dedicated to Saint Michael and, in time, to Saint Gudula as well, is the origin of the twin-towered cathedral that still stands in Brussels today.
Saint Michael, the dragon slayer, became the other patron of the city, and he stands on top of the town hall, as we will see.
By this point, the pieces were in place.
There was a lowland market settlement on the river, where merchants and craftsmen gathered.
There was a church on the hill, with wealth and influence.
There was a castle for protection.
And there was a ruling family, the counts of Leuven, who increasingly saw this place as an important part of their growing territory.
Around the year 1100, the people of Brussels built their first defensive wall, a modest circuit around the main settlement.
Inside, the town was small, perhaps a few thousand people.
They made cloth, baked bread, brewed beer, and traded.
It was not yet a great city. But it was now a real town, with walls, a market, a church, and a lord.
And it was about to enter a time of rapid growth.

In the next chapter, the counts of Leuven become dukes, the craftsmen of Brussels organize themselves into powerful guilds, and a muddy market square begins its transformation into one of the most famous squares in the world.
